title: Sudoku Solver & Validator
summary: A pure constraint-satisfaction case study with no players or turns — just rows, columns, and boxes modeled as one reusable Region, plus a backtracking solver.

slides.markdown:
"Design a Sudoku validator" and "design a Sudoku solver" are two different interviews wearing the same puzzle. A validator checks that a *completed* (or partially-filled) grid breaks no rules — no search involved. A solver has to *find* a valid completion, which means backtracking search.

Confirm which one you're being asked for in the first minute — the entity model (Grid, Cell, Region) is shared, but the algorithmic core is completely different, and guessing wrong wastes half the interview.

There are no players or turns here — it's a pure constraint-satisfaction problem over one static grid.

**In scope:** a 9x9 grid of digits 1-9, with three overlapping constraints — every row has each digit exactly once, every column has each digit exactly once, every 3x3 box has each digit exactly once. A **validator** checks whether the current grid (fully or partially filled) violates any constraint. A **solver** additionally fills empty cells to produce a complete, valid grid.

Treat these as **separate scopes** you can be asked for independently: a validator alone is a 15-minute exercise in modeling constraints cleanly; a solver adds a genuine algorithm (backtracking, optionally with pruning) on top. Confirm which is wanted, and whether cells can be empty (denoted 0 or blank) in the validator's input.

Three entities. **Cell** holds a digit (or empty) at a fixed row/column. **Grid** owns the 9x9 array of cells. **Region** is the key abstraction — a group of exactly 9 cells that must all contain distinct digits. A row is a Region. A column is a Region. Each 3x3 box is a Region.

The insight worth stating explicitly: **every cell belongs to exactly three Regions simultaneously** — its row, its column, and its box. Modeling `Region` as one reusable concept, rather than writing separate row-check/column-check/box-check code, is what turns three special cases into one piece of logic applied three times.

slides.markdown:
![A 9x9 Sudoku grid highlighting one cell as the overlap point of its row, column, and 3x3 box](assets/region-membership.svg)

Every cell in the grid has exactly this same triple membership — the highlighted cell is not special, it's representative. That uniformity is exactly why `Region` can be one class instead of three.

slides.sectionTitle: The hard part: one Region abstraction, not three checks
slides.markdown:
The naive design writes `checkRows()`, `checkColumns()`, and `checkBoxes()` as three separate methods, each with its own loop and its own duplicate-detection logic copy-pasted three times. That's fragile: a bug fix in duplicate-detection has to be applied in three places, and a variant puzzle (§ extending) needs a fourth near-identical method.

The fix is designing `Region` as **one abstraction reused for all three constraint types** — a `Region` doesn't know or care whether it represents a row, column, or box; it only knows "these 9 coordinates must hold 9 distinct digits." `Grid` just builds 27 `Region` instances up front and treats them identically forever after.

This is the same generalize-the-repeated-shape instinct as [WinChecker](tic-tac-toe)'s line-generation in Tic-Tac-Toe.

![Backtracking search tree branching per candidate digit, with dead ends backtracking and one branch reaching a solved leaf](assets/backtracking-tree.svg)

Each node change is one digit placed in one empty cell; each dead end is a constraint violation caught immediately, not after filling the whole grid. The depth of the tree is bounded by the number of empty cells — at most 81.

assets.alt: Backtracking search tree branching per candidate digit, with dead ends backtracking and one branch reaching a solved leaf

slides.sectionTitle: Code: backtracking solve with early pruning
Compare: brute-force backtracking vs constraint propagation
slides.markdown:
| | Plain backtracking | Constraint propagation (naked singles/pairs) |
|---|---|---|
| Idea | Try each digit, recurse, undo on failure | Before guessing, deduce cells that have only one possible digit left (naked single) or narrow candidate sets using pairs |
| Speed | Correct but can explore many dead branches on hard puzzles | Dramatically prunes the search space before any guessing starts |
| Complexity to implement | Low — one recursive function | Higher — needs per-cell candidate tracking, updated incrementally |

**How to decide:** plain backtracking is the right interview answer when asked to "design a solver" from scratch — it's correct and explainable in the time available. Mention constraint propagation as the natural follow-up optimization if asked how to make it faster on genuinely hard puzzles.

Sudoku-X adds the two main diagonals as additional Regions (each must also hold 9 distinct digits). Killer Sudoku replaces or adds "cage" Regions — irregularly-shaped groups of cells that must sum to a given total, in addition to (or instead of) the standard uniqueness constraint.

Because `Region` was designed as "a set of cells with a rule to check," both variants are new `Region` implementations — a `DiagonalRegion` or a `CageRegion` — added to `allRegions` at construction. `Grid.isValid()` and the backtracking `solve()` don't change at all; they already iterate over whatever regions exist and ask each one "are you satisfied."

This is a live instance of the [Strategy pattern](strategy-pattern): each Region type is a pluggable rule-checking strategy behind one interface.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: re-scanning the whole grid on every update
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To check if a move is legal, I'll just re-run `isValid()` on the whole grid after placing each digit."

**Why it's wrong:** re-validating all 27 regions after every single-cell change is needless work — a newly placed digit can only violate the **three regions that cell belongs to** (its row, column, box), exactly like Tic-Tac-Toe's win-check only needing to inspect lines through the last move. On a solver doing thousands of placements during backtracking, this difference is the gap between a solver that finishes in milliseconds and one that visibly stalls on hard puzzles.

**Correct model:** `canPlace(cell, digit)` checks only that cell's three regions — a small, constant amount of work — never the full grid.
